p.src: Now, when Xifeng returned to her room and found that Jia Lian was not yet back, she assigned tasks to the servants responsible for preparing Tanchun's luggage and trousseau. It was already past dusk when Tanchun suddenly came to mind, and Xifeng decided to go and see her. She called Feng'er and two maids to accompany her, with one maid walking ahead carrying a lantern. When they stepped outside, the moon had risen, bathing everything in a watery radiance. Xifeng told the maid with the lantern, “Go back.” As she passed beneath the window of the tea room, she heard people whispering inside; they seemed at once to be crying, laughing, and discussing something. Xifeng knew it could only be the household matrons stirring up some fresh gossip. Thoroughly displeased, she ordered Xiaohong to go in, pretend she had happened by, listen carefully, and draw out the whole story through discreet questioning. Xiaohong acknowledged the order and went in. Taking only Feng'er with her, Xifeng reached the garden gate. It had not yet been shut, but stood loosely closed. Mistress and maid pushed open the gate and entered. The moonlight within the garden seemed even brighter than outside; overlapping shadows of trees covered the ground, and with not a human voice to be heard, the place was bleak and still. Just as they were about to take the path toward Autumn Freshness Studio, a sudden gust swept by. Fallen leaves rustled all across the garden, the treetops whistled and creaked, and the roosting crows and other birds took frightened flight. Xifeng had been drinking, and when the wind struck her, she began to shiver. Feng'er too hunched her head into her shoulders and exclaimed, “How cold!” Unable to bear it either, Xifeng told her, “Hurry back and fetch my silver-squirrel waistcoat. I'll wait for you at Third Sister's.” Feng'er could not have wished for a better order, for she too wanted to go back and put on more clothes. She answered and immediately turned and ran off.

p.src: Xifeng had taken only a few steps when she heard snuffling and panting behind her, as though something were sniffing at her. Her hair stood on end. She could not help turning to look and saw a pitch-black creature behind her, stretching out its muzzle to sniff her, its two eyes glowing like lanterns. Terrified out of her wits, Xifeng involuntarily let out a startled cough. It was only a large dog. The dog jerked back its head, turned around, and, trailing a broom-like tail, raced straight up the great earthen hill. There it stopped, turned, and even raised its forepaws toward Xifeng. Her heart pounding and her senses reeling, Xifeng hurried toward Autumn Freshness Studio. She had nearly reached the entrance when, just as she rounded a rockery, a human figure flickered before her. Puzzled, Xifeng supposed it must be a maid from one of the other apartments and called, “Who is it?” She called twice, but no one appeared, and by then terror had sent her wits wandering. In her daze, she seemed to hear someone behind her say, “Aunt, do you no longer recognize even me?” Xifeng hastily turned and saw a pretty, elegantly dressed woman who looked exceedingly familiar, though she could not recall of which household or apartment she was the young wife. The woman continued, “Aunt, you were so intent on enjoying splendor and wealth that you cast into the Eastern Ocean everything I once told you about laying a foundation that would endure for ten thousand years.” At these words Xifeng lowered her head and searched her memory, but still could not place her. The woman sneered, “How dearly you cherished me then, Aunt, yet now you have forgotten me beyond the highest clouds.” Only then did Xifeng realize that it was Qin-shi, Jia Rong's late wife. She cried, “Good heavens! You're dead! What are you doing here?” She spat, then turned around, but unexpectedly caught her foot on a stone and fell. It was as though she had awakened from a dream, and sweat poured from her whole body like rain. Though every hair still bristled, her mind had cleared, and she saw the indistinct figures of Xiaohong and Feng'er approaching. Afraid of giving people cause to criticize her, Xifeng scrambled up and said, “What have you two been doing, taking so long? Hurry and give it to me so I can put it on.” Feng'er came forward and helped her put it on, while Xiaohong supported her. Xifeng said, “I had only just reached their place, but they were all asleep. Let us go back.” As she spoke, she led the two maids hurriedly back to her quarters. Jia Lian had returned, but she saw that his expression was unusually altered. She wanted to ask him about it, yet knowing his usual temper, she dared not question him abruptly and could only go to bed. At the fifth watch the next morning, Jia Lian rose to visit the home of Qiu Shi'an, the Chief Inspector Eunuch of the Inner Court, and make inquiries.

p.src: Since it was still too early, he noticed on the table a court gazette delivered the previous day, picked it up, and idly began to read. The first item was a memorial from Wang Zhong, Military Commissioner of Yunnan, reporting the recent capture of a group attempting to smuggle muskets and gunpowder beyond the frontier; there were eighteen offenders in all. The first of them, Bao Yin, claimed to be a servant of Jia Hua, Grand Preceptor and Duke Who Secures the Realm. The second was a memorial from Li Xiao, Prefect of Suzhou, impeaching a man for letting his household slave run unchecked and abuse soldiers and civilians by relying on his master's influence, ultimately murdering three members of a virtuous woman's family after failing to violate her. The murderer was named Shi Fu and claimed to be a servant of Jia Fan, hereditary holder of a third-rank title. Reading these two reports, Jia Lian's uneasiness returned at once. He was about to read the third, but feared that if he delayed he would miss Qiu Shi'an. He therefore dressed in haste without waiting for anything to eat. Just then Ping'er brought him tea; after taking two sips, he went out, mounted his horse, and rode away.

p.src: Pinger was in the room putting away the clothes that had been changed. Xifeng had not yet risen. Pinger said, “I heard that you scarcely slept at all last night, madam. Let me massage you now, and have a good nap.” Xifeng said nothing for some time. Taking her silence for consent, Pinger climbed onto the kang, sat beside her, and began gently massaging her. She had given only a few strokes when Xifeng was just beginning to drift off, and they heard little Dajie crying in the other room. Xifeng opened her eyes again, and Pinger promptly called toward the other room, “Nurse Li, what on earth are you doing? The little girl is crying. Pat her and soothe her. You really do sleep too soundly.” Nurse Li woke with a start from her dream. Hearing Pinger speak to her in this way, she was inwardly annoyed, but had no choice except to pat the child several times with great force, grumbling as she cursed, “You truly are a short-lived little wretch! Instead of lying still like a corpse, you howl as though mourning your mother in the dead of night!” As she spoke, she gritted her teeth and gave the child a hard pinch. The child burst into loud wails. Hearing this, Xifeng exclaimed, “This is outrageous! Listen to that—she must be tormenting the child. Go over there, give that black-hearted, man-keeping hag a few blows with all your might, and bring my little girl here.” Pinger smiled. “Please don’t be angry, madam. She would never dare torment the little girl. Perhaps she merely knocked against her by accident. It would be easy enough to beat her now, but tomorrow they would gossip behind our backs and say we struck servants in the middle of the night.” Xifeng heard her out and remained silent for a long while. Then she heaved a deep sigh and said, “Look at me—even now, am I not still at the very height of my power? If I should die tomorrow, who knows what will become of this little bane I leave behind!” Pinger said with a smile, “Why would you say such a thing, madam? Why talk like this before dawn?” Xifeng gave a cold laugh. “What would you know? I understood it long ago. I have not much longer to live. Though I have lived only twenty-five years, I have seen what others never see and tasted what others never taste. I may count my life as complete. I have had everything this world has to offer. I have vented every grievance and fought for every advantage. If all I lack is a little longevity, so be it.” At these words, Pinger could not keep the tears from rolling down her cheeks. Xifeng smiled. “There is no need to feign compassion now. When I die, all of you will only rejoice. You can all live together in perfect harmony, without having me forever pricking your eyes like a thorn. I ask only one thing: if you have any sense of right and wrong, be sure to cherish my child.” When Pinger heard this, she wept all the harder until she was drenched in tears.

p.src: Pinger had just climbed down from the kang and was about to leave when she heard footsteps outside. As it happened, Jia Lian had arrived too late: Qiu Shi’an had already gone to court. Having returned without meeting him and in a thoroughly bad temper, Jia Lian entered and asked Pinger, “Have those people still not got up?” “No, they haven’t,” Pinger replied. Jia Lian flung aside each curtain as he came in and sneered, “Good, very good! Still none of them up at this hour—they mean to defy me outright and wash their hands of everything!” Then he repeatedly called for tea. Pinger hurriedly poured him a bowl of tea. The maids and old women, seeing Jia Lian leave the house, had gone back to sleep. They had not expected him to return so soon and had prepared nothing. Pinger therefore brought him some tea that had been warmed over. In a rage, Jia Lian raised the bowl and dashed it to the floor, where it shattered with a crash.

p.src: Xifeng awoke with a start, drenched in cold sweat. With a cry of alarm she opened her eyes and saw Jia Lian sitting beside her in a fury, while Ping'er bent down to pick up the shards of a bowl. “Why are you back already?” Xifeng asked. She asked once, but when he gave no answer for a long while, she had to ask again. Jia Lian shouted, “You don't want me back? Then let me die out there!” Xifeng smiled. “Why make such a fuss? You don't usually return as quickly as you did today. I merely asked you about it—there's no reason to be angry.” Jia Lian shouted again, “I didn't find him, so why shouldn't I come straight back?” Xifeng smiled. “If you didn't find him, you'll simply have to be patient. Go earlier tomorrow and you'll be sure to meet him.” Jia Lian cried, “I'm not going to live at my own expense while running myself ragged for someone else. I've a mountain of my own business that hasn't even begun to move, yet for no good reason I've spent all these days bustling blindly over another man's affairs. What's the point? The very man whose trouble it is sits comfortably at home without a care for what happens, and I even hear he's planning a birthday celebration with deafening gongs and drums, a banquet, and theatricals. And I'm supposed to run my damned legs off for him!” As he spoke, he spat on the floor and then cursed Ping'er as well. Hearing this, Xifeng choked with anger. She was about to argue with him, but after a moment's thought restrained herself and forced a smile. “Why get into such a rage and shout at me first thing in the morning? Who told you to promise to help them? Since you did promise, you must be patient and see the matter through for them. Still, I never heard of anyone facing serious trouble himself yet remaining in the mood to put on plays and hold banquets!” “Exactly!” said Jia Lian. “You should ask him about it tomorrow!” Xifeng asked in surprise, “Ask whom?” “Whom?” said Jia Lian. “Your brother.” “Is it he?” asked Xifeng. “Of course it is. Who else could it be?” replied Jia Lian. Xifeng hurriedly asked, “What trouble has he got into now, that he needs you to run about for him?” “So you're still completely in the dark,” said Jia Lian. “Now that truly is strange,” said Xifeng. “I haven't heard a single word about it.” “How could you know?” said Jia Lian. “Even Her Ladyship and your aunt know nothing about it. First, I was afraid it would worry them; second, you've so often complained of being unwell. So I kept the affair suppressed outside and let no one in the inner quarters hear of it. The very mention of it is infuriating! If you hadn't asked me today, I wouldn't have felt free to tell you. Do you imagine your brother behaves like a decent human being? Do you know what people outside call him?” “What do they call him?” asked Xifeng.

p.src: “What do they call him?” said Jia Lian. “They call him ‘Wang-ren—the man who has forgotten benevolence’!” Xifeng burst out laughing. “Well, if he isn't called Wang Ren, what else should they call him?” “You think I mean the name Wang Ren?” said Jia Lian. “I mean ‘Wang-ren’ as in one who has forgotten benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and good faith!” “Who could be so spiteful as to malign him like that?” asked Xifeng. “Malign him?” said Jia Lian. “Today I'll tell you everything, so that you may learn what a fine brother you have. You do know that he's giving a birthday celebration for his second uncle, don't you?” After thinking for a moment, Xifeng said, “Oh, yes! I forgot to ask you—isn't Second Uncle's birthday in winter? I remember Baoyu goes there every year. When the Master was promoted some time ago, Second Uncle sent a theatrical troupe here, and I remarked in private that Second Uncle was exceedingly miserly and could not compare with Eldest Uncle. The members of their own household are always glaring at one another like fighting cocks. Why, when Eldest Uncle died recently, though Second Uncle was his own brother, did he ever step forward and take charge of a single thing? That was why I said the other day that on his birthday we should return the courtesy by sending him a theatrical troupe, so that we wouldn't appear indebted before the rest of the family. I can't understand why they're celebrating his birthday so early now.” “You're still dreaming,” said Jia Lian. As soon as he reached the capital, he seized upon the unsettled business left by your uncle's death and opened a subscription. He kept it from us for fear we'd stop him, and collected several thousand taels of silver. Later, your second uncle reproached him, saying he shouldn't have swept everything into his net. Unable to withstand the pressure, he devised another scheme and cast his net in the name of your second uncle's birthday, hoping to raise more money to placate him. He cared nothing whether the birthday was in winter or summer, or whether their relatives and friends knew the true date. What a disgrace! Do you know why I rose so early? Because of the present trouble on the maritime frontier, a censor has submitted an impeachment stating that the deficit left by Eldest Uncle, now deceased, should be made good by his younger brother Wang Zisheng and his nephew Wang Ren. Uncle and nephew panicked and came to me, asking me to use my connections on their behalf. Seeing how terrified they were, and since the affair also concerns Her Ladyship and you, I agreed to help. I intended to seek out Old Qiu, the Chief Inspector in charge of the Inner Court, and ask him to manage matters—perhaps by shifting the deficit between the former and present officeholders. But I happened to arrive too late; he'd already gone inside, so I got up early and made the journey for nothing. Meanwhile, their household is still busy booking theatricals and arranging a banquet. Tell me, is that enough to make a man angry or not?”

But I happened to arrive too late; he'd already gone inside, so I got up early and made the journey for nothing.
Meanwhile, their household is still busy booking theatricals and arranging a banquet.
Tell me, is that enough to make a man angry or not?”

p.src: Only after hearing this did Xifeng learn how Wang Ren had behaved. But proud and fiercely protective of her own as she was, when she heard Jia Lian speak so, she said, “Whatever he may be like, he is still your own elder brother-in-law. Besides, in this matter both the late First Master and the living Second Uncle would be grateful to you. Very well, there is nothing more to say. Since it concerns my family, I suppose I must humble myself and beg you, lest others suffer on my account and curse me behind my back.” As she spoke, tears were already streaming down her face. She threw back the covers and sat up, gathering her hair with one hand while putting on her clothes with the other. Jia Lian said, “There is no need for you to behave like this. It is your brother who has behaved disgracefully; I said nothing against you. Besides, I had gone out, and you were unwell; yet even after I had risen, they were all still asleep. Did our elders ever permit such a rule in this household? Now you have turned into a complacent peacemaker and no longer manage anything. I say one word and you immediately get up; if tomorrow I find fault with those servants, are you going to take their place too? How utterly pointless!” Only after hearing this did Xifeng stop her tears and say, “It is no longer early; I ought to get up anyway. Since you say so, if you will take their family’s affair to heart and see it properly handled, that will be a great kindness from you. Besides, it is not only for my sake; Her Ladyship will be pleased when she hears of it too.” Jia Lian said, “All right, I understand. ‘As if a great radish still needed manure poured over it!’” Pinger said, “Why should you rise so early, madam? Don’t you have a fixed time for getting up every day? I cannot imagine where Master picked up this perverse fit of anger, only to vent it on us. Why do this to yourself? You have surely done more than enough for Master; in what affair have you not stood in the front line for him? If I may say so, Master has enjoyed no end of ready-made benefits; now that he is doing one small thing for you—one that also concerns several branches of the family—he makes such a great show of reluctance. Is he not afraid of chilling people’s hearts? Besides, this is not merely your affair alone. If we rose late, Master was right to be angry; after all, we are servants. But you have exhausted yourself in Master’s service until you are nothing but a bundle of ailments. Why must you suffer so?” As she spoke, her own eyes reddened too. Jia Lian had been full of pent-up anger, but how could he withstand the words of this lovely wife and beautiful concubine, at once sharp and tender? He laughed and said, “Enough, let it go. She alone is more than enough; there is no need for you to help her. In any case, I am the outsider here. Whenever I die, you two will finally have peace.” Xifeng said, “Do not say such things. Who knows what fate awaits any of us? You may not die before I do. The sooner I die, the sooner my heart will be at peace.”

p.src: Meanwhile, Xifeng had risen and was washing and dressing when a young maid from Lady Wang’s quarters suddenly came in and said, “Her Ladyship has sent me to ask whether Second Mistress intends to visit your honored uncle today. If you do, Her Ladyship says that Second Mistress Bao is to go together with you.” After the exchange just past, Xifeng was already disheartened and despondent, resentful that her natal family had failed to acquit itself with credit. Added to this was the fright she had suffered in the garden the night before, and she truly had no energy. So she said, “Go back and tell Her Ladyship that I still have one or two matters left unsettled and cannot go today. Besides, what they are doing there is hardly any proper business. If Second Mistress Bao wishes to go, she may go on her own.” The young maid acknowledged the instruction, went back, and delivered the reply. There is no more to be said of this.

p.src: Now, after Fengjie had combed her hair and changed her clothes, she reflected that although she would not be going herself, she ought at least to send word. Besides, Baochai was still a new bride, so when she went out, Fengjie naturally ought to see that everything was properly attended to. She therefore went to see Lady Wang, made some excuse about a matter, and then came over to Baoyu's room. There she found Baoyu dressed but reclining crookedly on the kang, his eyes fixed vacantly on Baochai as she combed her hair. Fengjie stood in the doorway until Baochai happened to turn and notice her, whereupon Baochai hurriedly rose and invited her to sit down. Baoyu scrambled up as well, and only then did Fengjie sit down with a beaming smile. Baochai reproached Sheyue, “You saw Second Mistress coming in, yet you did not say a word.” Sheyue replied with a smile, “But when Second Mistress first came in, did she not wave her hand to tell us to keep quiet?” Fengjie then said to Baoyu, “Why have you not left yet? What are you waiting for? I have never seen a grown man remain so childish. She is doing her hair; what are you doing sprawled beside her and staring? You spend every day together in this room—have you still not seen enough of her? Are you not afraid the maids will laugh at you?” At this she gave a snorting laugh, then looked him over and smacked her lips. Though Baoyu felt somewhat embarrassed, he paid her no heed. Baochai, however, blushed scarlet from sheer mortification; unable either to go on listening or to answer, she saw Xiren bring in tea and, merely to cover her confusion, took a tobacco pouch and handed it over herself. Fengjie rose smiling to take it and said, “Second Cousin, never mind our affairs. Hurry and get dressed.” Baoyu, likewise trying to hide his embarrassment, busied himself looking for one thing and fiddling with another. Fengjie said, “You go on ahead. What gentleman ever waits to set out together with the ladies?” Baoyu said, “It is only that I do not much care for these clothes. They are not as fine as that peacock-gold cloak Grandmother gave me, which I wore the year before last.” Fengjie teased him, “Then why do you not wear it?” Baoyu replied, “It is still too early in the season for it.” Fengjie suddenly remembered the cloak's history and regretted her careless question. Fortunately, Baochai was also closely related to the Wang family, though Fengjie still felt awkward before the maids. Xiren, however, took up the subject: “Second Mistress does not know—even if it were time to wear it, he would refuse.” “Why is that?” asked Fengjie. Xiren replied, “Let me tell you, Second Mistress: everything our young master does seems to fall straight out of the sky. That year, for Second Great-Uncle's birthday, Grandmother gave him that cloak, but somehow it was scorched that very day. My mother was gravely ill, so I was away from the house. Qingwen was still with us then. Though she was ill, when she heard what had happened, she spent the whole night mending it for him, so that the next day Grandmother noticed nothing.”

p.src: Last year, on a cold day when he was going to school, I told Beiming to take it along for him to throw over his shoulders. But when our young master saw the cloak, it reminded him of Qingwen. He declared he would never wear it again and ordered me to keep it for him all my life.” Before Xiren had finished, Fengjie broke in: “Now that you mention Qingwen, what a pity she was! The child had both a pretty face and clever hands; only her tongue was a little too sharp. Yet, for no good reason, Her Ladyship listened to some rumor from who knows where and hounded the poor child to her death. There is something else. The other day I saw the daughter of Liu's wife from the kitchen—what was her name, Wuer? That girl looks for all the world like Qingwen's very shadow. I wanted to bring her in here, and when I later asked her mother, she said she would be delighted. I thought that since Xiaohong from Second Master Bao's room had come away with me and I had never sent anyone back in her place, I might fill the vacancy with Wuer. But Ping'er said that Her Ladyship had once declared that no girl resembling that sort was ever to be assigned to Second Master Bao's room. So I let the matter drop. But now that Second Master Bao is married, what is there left to fear? I may as well bring her in. I only wonder whether Second Master Bao would like that. Whenever you miss Qingwen, you need only look at Wuer.” Baoyu had been about to leave, but on hearing this, he stood transfixed. Xiren said, “Why would he not want her? We meant to bring her here long ago; it was only Her Ladyship's firm prohibition that stopped us.” “In that case,” said Fengjie, “I shall have her brought in tomorrow. I shall answer to Her Ladyship.” Baoyu was beside himself with joy on hearing this, and only then went over to Grandmother Jia's quarters. Meanwhile, Baochai put on her clothes. Seeing how tenderly devoted the young couple were to each other, Fengjie remembered Jia Lian's behavior toward her just now and felt unbearably heartsick. Unable to remain seated, she rose and said to Baochai with a smile, “Let us go together to Grandmother's rooms.” Smiling, she left the room, and the two of them went together to see Grandmother Jia.

p.src: Baoyu was just then asking Grandmother Jia's permission to visit his uncle's home. Grandmother Jia nodded and said, “Go, then, but drink little and come home early. You have only just begun to recover.” Baoyu assented and went out, but no sooner had he reached the courtyard than he turned back and whispered something in Baochai's ear. Baochai smiled. “Yes, I understand. Hurry along now.” With that, she urged Baoyu on his way. Grandmother Jia had exchanged scarcely three sentences with Xifeng and Baochai when Qiuwen came in with a message: “Second Master has sent Biming back to ask for Second Mistress.” Baochai said, “What has he forgotten now, that he has sent him back again?” Qiuwen replied, “I sent a little maid to ask. Biming said, ‘Second Master forgot to say something and sent me back to tell Second Mistress: if you're coming, please hurry; if you're not, don't stand about in the wind.’” At this, Grandmother Jia, Xifeng, and all the old serving-women and maids standing below burst out laughing. Baochai's face flushed crimson. She spat playfully at Qiuwen and said, “What a muddle-headed creature! Was that worth rushing back in such a fluster to report?” Laughing too, Qiuwen went back and told the little maid to give Biming a scolding. As Biming ran on, he looked back and called, “Second Master went out of his way to call me down from my horse and send me back with that message. If I hadn't delivered it, he would have questioned me when I returned and scolded me again. Now that I have delivered it, they scold me instead!” The maid ran back laughing and repeated what he had said. Grandmother Jia said to Baochai, “You had better go, so that he need not worry about you so.” Baochai could endure the teasing no longer; and when Xifeng joined in to make sport of her, she grew too embarrassed to remain and finally left.

p.src: Just then, the nun Daliao from Scattered Flowers Temple arrived. She paid her respects to Grandmother Jia, greeted Xifeng, and sat down to take tea. Grandmother Jia asked her, “Why have you not visited us lately?” Daliao replied, “We have been holding religious services at the temple these past few days, and several titled ladies have been staying there from time to time, so I have had no leisure to come. I came especially today to inform you, Old Ancestress, that another family will hold a service tomorrow. If it pleases you, perhaps you might come and share in the merit.” Grandmother Jia asked, “What sort of service are they holding?” Daliao said, “Last month, Lord Wang's residence was plagued by unclean presences and apparitions; and as ill luck would have it, the lady of the house saw her late husband one night. So yesterday she told me at the temple that she wished to make a vow and burn incense before the Bodhisattva of Scattered Flowers, and to hold a forty-nine-day Water-and-Land Rite, praying that her household might be safe, the dead ascend to Heaven, and the living receive blessings. That is why I have had no time to come and pay my respects to you, Old Madam.” Now Xifeng had always detested such matters, but ever since seeing a ghost the previous night, she had remained full of doubt and unease. Hearing Daliao's words, she unconsciously abandoned half her habitual skepticism and became somewhat inclined to believe. She therefore asked, “Who is this Bodhisattva of Scattered Flowers? How can this deity ward off evil and drive away ghosts?” Perceiving from the question that Xifeng was beginning to believe, Daliao replied, “Since you ask me today, madam, allow me to explain it to you. The Bodhisattva of Scattered Flowers has no ordinary origin, and possesses extraordinary spiritual attainment. The Bodhisattva was born in the Great Tree Kingdom of the Western Heaven, to parents who made their living gathering firewood. At birth, the Bodhisattva had three horns upon the head, four eyes set crosswise, a body three feet tall, and hands that trailed upon the ground. The parents declared the child a demon and abandoned it behind an icy mountain. But on that mountain lived an old monkey who had attained the Way. Coming out in search of food, he saw white vapor soaring skyward from the Bodhisattva's head and tigers and wolves keeping their distance. Knowing that the child was no ordinary being, he carried it back to his cave and reared it. The Bodhisattva proved innately wise and could discourse upon Chan. Every day the Bodhisattva and the monkey discussed the Way and contemplated Chan, until celestial flowers fell about them in profusion. After a thousand years, the Bodhisattva ascended to Heaven. Even today, celestial flowers may still be seen scattered over the place on the mountain where the scriptures were expounded. Every prayer is answered, and the Bodhisattva often manifests to deliver people from suffering and calamity. That is why people built a temple, fashioned an image, and enshrined the Bodhisattva.” Xifeng asked, “What proof is there of any of this?” Daliao replied, “There you go raising objections again, madam. What proof can one expect for a Buddha? Even if it were a lie, it could deceive only one or two people. Surely all the wise people from ancient times to the present cannot have been deceived by it? Just consider, madam: only the incense fires of Buddhism have endured unbroken through the ages. It must be because Buddhism blesses the nation and its people and has shown some efficacy that people have placed their faith in it.”

p.src: Xifeng found this most reasonable and said, “In that case, I shall go and put it to the test tomorrow. Do you have fortune sticks at your temple? If I draw one, can its interpretation reveal what is troubling me? If it can, I shall believe from that day forward.” Daliao replied, “Our fortune sticks are extraordinarily efficacious. Come and draw one tomorrow, madam, and you will see.” Grandmother Jia said, “If that is so, you might as well wait until the day after tomorrow, the first of the month, before going to draw one.” After this, Daliao finished her tea, went to pay her respects to Lady Wang and the ladies in the other apartments, and then returned to the temple, of which no more need be said.

p.src: Even after reading it, she could make little sense of it. Daliao said, “This is cause for great joy, madam. This lot is remarkably apt. You have lived here since childhood, madam, and have never once returned to Nanjing. Now that the Master has received an appointment in the provinces, he may send for his family, and you could return home on the way. Would that not be ‘returning home clad in glory’?” As she spoke, she copied out the lot’s interpretation and handed it to a maid. Xifeng remained half doubtful and half convinced. Daliao had a vegetarian meal laid out, but Xifeng merely touched a morsel, then set it down and rose to leave, giving an offering for incense as well. Daliao urged her earnestly to stay, but could not detain her and had no choice but to let her go. When Xifeng returned home and saw Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, and the others, they asked about the lot and had someone interpret it. All were delighted. “Perhaps the Master truly does intend this. It would be good for us to make the journey.” Hearing everyone say the same, Xifeng came to believe it too. But no more need be said of this.

p.src: Now Baoyu had been taking his afternoon nap that day. When he awoke and did not see Baochai, he was just about to ask after her when she came in. Baoyu asked, “Where have you been? I haven’t seen you for ages.” Baochai smiled. “I went to look over a fortune-telling lot for Cousin Xifeng.” At this, Baoyu asked what sort of lot it was. Baochai recited the inscription on the lot, then added, “Everyone in the household says it is auspicious. But in my view, there is more behind those words ‘returning home clad in glory.’ We shall wait and see what comes of them.” Baoyu said, “You are being suspicious again and recklessly misinterpreting the divine message. From ancient times to the present, everyone has known that ‘returning home clad in glory’ is auspicious, yet today you alone insist on finding some hidden cause in it. According to you, what other meaning could ‘returning home clad in glory’ possibly have?” Baochai was just about to explain when a maid sent by Lady Wang came to summon the Second Young Mistress. Baochai went over at once. What the matter was will be revealed in the next chapter.
